title: Wait!? Are You Cheating or NOT? | Sicilian Defense | GM Naroditsky’s Top Theory Speedrun

moves.spoken: Nc3 is the doorway to the anti-Sicilians — the Grand Prix with f4, the Closed with g3, or a transposition straight back into an Open Sicilian.
moves.teaches: Nc3 keeps every anti-Sicilian and the Open Sicilian in White's back pocket.

moves.spoken: As Accelerated Dragon players we answer Nc6 — though a Najdorf player should avoid it here, since White can move-order you into a system you don't play.
moves.teaches: Match your move-two choice to the Open Sicilian you actually play, or risk being transposed out of your book.

moves.spoken: Bb5 is a faceless anti-Sicilian — it looks like a Rossolimo but is inferior, because d4 is left unguarded: the knight that would defend it never comes to f3.
moves.teaches: Bb5 without a knight developed to f3 concedes d4; that missing guard is the flaw to exploit.

moves.spoken: The principled reply is Nd4 — the same motif you'd use against a Trompowsky bishop: the knight becomes a monster in the centre and hits the bishop at once.
moves.teaches: Meet a pinning bishop by leaping the knight to d4, gaining a central monster and attacking the bishop.

moves.spoken: We swap the knight for the bishop. Now a6 is the human instinct, but it's worth questioning your instincts — the b5-knight isn't dangerous on its own, so d6 or Nf6 hitting the loose e4-pawn are real options too.
moves.teaches: Don't play the automatic pawn-kick reflexively; a stray enemy knight often isn't worth the tempo.

moves.spoken: Even after cxd4 this stays an anti-Sicilian — White has no light-squared bishop, so it's a different animal from a Najdorf. Our one problem is that we're badly behind in development.
moves.teaches: Read the position by what's missing: no light bishop means it's not a real Open Sicilian.

moves.spoken: Nf6 would run into e5, so we head that off — sometimes you accept a small positional concession rather than get crushed while undeveloped.
moves.teaches: Concede a little structurally to prevent a central break that would punish your lack of development.

moves.spoken: h6 stops Bg5 — the Smyslov idea of trading the knight and then planting one on d5. We have to keep a knight available to contest that square.
moves.teaches: Prevent the trade that would surrender d5; contesting the outpost is worth a pawn move.

moves.spoken: Now we finally develop with Nf6; if Bb6, Qd7 is a fine, if slightly awkward, answer, and the queen can reroute to c6 later to free the bishop.

Under pressure the queen must go to e6 — the only square that keeps e5 defended, since otherwise Nxe5 crashes in. Conducting an initiative cleanly is one of the hardest skills in chess, and it cuts both ways.
moves.teaches: When defending, find the one square that holds your key point; sustaining an attack is hard even for the attacker.
